issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside a court-conducted sale for obvious and manifest illegality despite the absence of a timely application under the ordinary sale-challenge procedure.
material_facts: A court receiver conducted the sale, which was approved by a single judge.
The sale process involved orders made in chambers, and higher offers were not properly scrutinised or considered.
The appellant argued that an application under the ordinary sale-challenge procedure had to be filed within limitation.
The Supreme Court took judicial notice of the illegality identified by the Division Bench and held that the sale and its confirmation were invalid.
issues.conclusion: The sale and its confirmation were set aside notwithstanding the argument that a timely procedural application was required.
issues.legal_principle: A court or appellate court need not remain a mute or helpless spectator to obvious and manifest illegality in a court sale. Order 21 Rules 89 and 90 and Section 48 CPC were cited as the basis of the appellant’s procedural argument, but the Court held that the manifest illegality could be addressed notwithstanding that argument. No earlier cases were cited.

predicates.court_sale_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a sale conducted by a court or its receiver.
predicates.manifest_sale_irregularity: The sale was conducted through a process that displayed obvious and manifest illegality, including inadequate judicial scrutiny of competing offers.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a court-conducted sale and the process displays manifest irregularity, the sale may be set aside without a timely procedural application.

issues.legal_issue: A court sale vitiated by inadequate scrutiny of competing offers must be conducted afresh by open auction after due publication.
material_facts: The Division Bench observed that there were higher offers but they were not adequately scrutinised.
The Supreme Court held that the circumstances vitiated the sale and its confirmation.
The Court remanded the matter for the appropriate judge to conduct a sale by open auction after due publication, giving intending bidders an opportunity to participate.
issues.conclusion: The sale was to be conducted afresh by open auction after due publication.
issues.legal_principle: A court-supervised sale must involve due application of mind to competing offers and provide intending bidders an opportunity to participate through an open auction after due publication. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited as the basis for this direction.

predicates.court_supervised_sale: The proceeding involves a sale supervised or conducted by a court or its receiver.
predicates.competing_offers_not_properly_scrutinise: Competing offers were not adequately scrutinised by the court before the sale was approved.

issues.definition: When a court-supervised sale proceeds without adequate scrutiny of competing offers, the fresh sale must be open and duly publicised.

issues.legal_issue: A court sale is illegal when the purchaser pays only part of the price and the balance is to be paid only after delivery of possession.
material_facts: The appellant had deposited only part of the purchase price.
The balance was assured to be deposited only after delivery of possession.
The Supreme Court held that this arrangement was also illegal.
issues.conclusion: The arrangement making payment of the balance conditional on delivery of possession was illegal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court expressly held that the arrangement to deposit the balance only after delivery of possession was illegal. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this holding.

predicates.court_sale: The proceeding involves a sale conducted under court supervision.
predicates.partial_payment_with_balance_due_only_af: The purchaser paid only part of the price and the remaining balance was to be paid only after delivery of possession.

issues.definition: When a purchaser in a court sale pays only part of the price and makes payment of the balance dependent on delivery of possession, that payment arrangement is illegal.

issues.legal_issue: A final preliminary decree in a foreclosure suit limits the scope of the suit and the sale made under it, while other rights or remedies must be pursued elsewhere.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned a foreclosure suit in which the preliminary decree had become final.
The Supreme Court directed that the sale be conducted pursuant to that decree and held that the parties could not widen the scope of the suit or the sale.
The Court stated that any other rights or remedies had to be worked out elsewhere and expressed no opinion on the respondents’ rights in the property.
issues.conclusion: The parties could not widen the scope of the foreclosure suit or the sale under the final preliminary decree; any other rights or remedies had to be pursued elsewhere.
issues.legal_principle: Where a preliminary decree in a foreclosure suit has become final, the scope of the suit and a sale pursuant to that decree cannot be widened; other rights or remedies must be pursued elsewhere. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this holding.

predicates.foreclosure_suit: The proceeding is a foreclosure suit.
predicates.preliminary_decree_final: The preliminary decree in the suit has become final.
predicates.party_seeks_to_expand_suit_or_sale: A party seeks to widen the scope of the suit or of a sale made pursuant to the decree.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to expand a foreclosure suit or sale after the preliminary decree has become final, any other rights or remedies must be pursued elsewhere.
